rationale: The recordings have no artifact rejection, so a few blinks, movement bursts or electrode pops can dominate the mean-averaged Welch spectrum, especially in the delta and gamma bands. This round makes one change: the per-segment spectra are averaged with the median instead of the mean (`average="median"`). The median ignores short artifact segments and should also make the features more robust on the external datasets from other clinics and amplifiers.

This round makes one change: each recording is re-referenced to the common average across the 19 channels before computing the PSD. Right now the relative-power features depend on each clinic's original reference, which is not the same in TDBRAIN and the external Mumtaz set. Average referencing removes the shared reference signal and makes the per-channel spectra comparable across amplifiers and montages. It should also sharpen local topography, such as frontal and parietal alpha/theta differences, which may help the dev score.

This round adds one feature: the aperiodic (1/f) exponent for each channel and condition. It is fitted as a log–log line to the same artifact-robust median Welch PSD over 2–40 Hz, leaving out the 7–14 Hz alpha peak. Depression has been linked to changes in the excitation/inhibition balance, and the 1/f slope is a proxy for that which relative band power only partly captures. The slope also doesn't depend on amplitude scale, which should help on the external datasets from other amplifiers.

This round adds one new feature family: individual alpha peak frequency per channel and condition, plus the height of the alpha peak above the 1/f fit. The peak frequency is a weighted average of 7–14 Hz, using only the power that sits above the aperiodic fit, and the height is the largest log-power excess over that fit. The current relative band powers mix the aperiodic background with the oscillatory alpha peak. Depression has been linked to a slower, altered alpha rhythm, and both new measures don't depend on amplitude scale, so they should carry over to other amplifiers.

This round adds one new feature family: per-channel functional connectivity. For each channel, condition and band, the feature is the Fisher-z magnitude-squared coherence with the other 18 channels, averaged into a "node strength". Depression is associated with altered large-scale synchrony, especially in fronto-parietal alpha and theta, which band power cannot capture. Coherence is also amplitude-scale invariant, so it should transfer to other amplifiers. Segments whose total power exceeds 3× the median are dropped, which keeps the cross-spectra artifact-robust.

The feature set has grown from about 100 to about 418 correlated features (relative power, 1/f slope and coherence for 2 conditions × 19 channels), but the L2 strength is still the arbitrary C=0.1. This round picks C by grouped inner CV on the training fold, optimising AUROC with the scaler refit inside each inner fold, so the regularisation fits the current dimensionality and sample size.

This round adds one feature family: per-channel, per-band node strength of the debiased weighted phase-lag index (wPLI) to the other channels. It is computed from the same artifact-screened 2-s segments as the coherence. Magnitude-squared coherence includes zero-lag coupling, which comes from volume conduction and the shared original reference. That probably also explains why average re-referencing hurt so much in round 2. wPLI counts only consistently lagged phase coupling, so it captures true interareal synchrony, which is reported to be altered in MDD. Like coherence, it does not depend on amplitude scale or on the reference montage, which should help on the external clinic.

This round adds one new feature family: Higuchi fractal dimension per channel and condition. It is computed on 1–45 Hz band-passed, non-overlapping 4-s epochs, and the median across epochs is kept. Several MDD EEG studies, including work on the Mumtaz data, report higher Higuchi fractal dimension in depression. It measures waveform complexity across time scales, which band power, 1/f slope and coherence do not capture. It doesn't depend on amplitude scale, and taking the median across epochs keeps it robust to artifacts on other amplifiers.

This round splits the relative band power into finer sub-bands: alpha into alpha1 (8–10 Hz) and alpha2 (10–13 Hz), and beta into beta1 (13–20 Hz) and beta2 (20–30 Hz). MDD findings are often specific to sub-bands (raised low-alpha and raised fast-beta power), and the broad 8–13 / 13–30 Hz bins blur these together. Coherence keeps the original 5 bands, so only 2×19×2 = 76 features are added. Like the current features, the new ones are log-relative, so they don't depend on amplitude scale.

This round changes the model, not the features. The 456 standardized features come from four families of very different sizes (relative power and coherence each have 190 columns; 1/f slope and Higuchi fractal dimension have 38 each). In a single L2 logistic regression the two large, correlated blocks take most of the weight. The new model averages the probabilities of the joint logistic regression with one logistic regression per family (late fusion), so each family's evidence counts equally. Averaging should also reduce variance at this small sample size.

This round adds one new feature family: EEG microstates. Microstates describe the order and timing of brain-wide topographies over time, which none of the current spectral, coherence or fractal features capture, and MDD studies report altered microstate coverage and duration. Four templates are found, without labels, by polarity-invariant k-means on artifact-screened GFP peaks pooled across all subjects. The data are band-passed to 2–20 Hz and average-referenced for this step only, so the existing features are unchanged. Each condition gets 16 new features: coverage, log mean duration, occurrence rate and explained variance for each of the four classes. All of them are amplitude-scale invariant.

Add per-channel Hjorth mobility and complexity for each condition. Both are log-transformed, computed on the same 1–45 Hz band-passed 4-s epochs as the Higuchi fractal dimension (FD), and summarized as the median over epochs. Hjorth parameters are among the most commonly reported time-domain MDD markers, including in work on the Mumtaz data. They are scale-invariant summaries of the waveform's mean frequency and bandwidth (spectral "sharpness"), which band sums, the 1/f slope, coherence and Higuchi FD don't capture. The block is small (76 features), so it shouldn't dilute the existing features the way the larger finer-band and wPLI blocks did.

This round adds one small, amplitude-invariant entropy block to the current features: normalized permutation entropy per channel (order 4, lag of about 8 ms, median over the 1–45 Hz 4-s epochs) and normalized spectral entropy of the median Welch PSD (1–45 Hz). MDD EEG studies, including work on the Mumtaz data, report changes in signal irregularity, and ordinal-pattern and spectral-flatness information is not directly captured by band sums, the 1/f slope, coherence, Higuchi FD or Hjorth. At 76 features the block is the same size as Hjorth, which helped, so it should not dilute the existing features.

This round adds one feature: each channel's log total 1–45 Hz power minus the mean across that subject's channels. The current power features are all relative within a channel, so they lose how amplitude is spread across the scalp. Re-centring on the subject's own mean keeps the scale independence that the external amplifier needs while restoring that spatial information. Together with the existing log-relative alpha, this also makes frontal alpha asymmetry (log absolute alpha F4 − F3), a classic MDD marker, available to the linear model. It adds only 38 features, so it shouldn't dilute the existing ones.

This round adds one feature: eyes-closed vs eyes-open reactivity, i.e. log(EC/EO) absolute power for each channel in each of the 5 bands. It is computed from the same median-averaged Welch spectra. Reduced alpha blocking (Berger effect) and changed reactivity are reported in MDD. The current per-condition relative powers cannot carry this, because they discard each condition's total power. Since the ratio is taken within one subject on one amplifier, it is still independent of amplitude scale, and the 95-feature block is about the size of the small blocks that helped before.

This round adds per-channel amplitude-envelope correlation (AEC) node strength in the theta and alpha bands. For each band, it takes the mean Fisher-z correlation of the log Hilbert envelope with the other 18 channels, using 4-s epochs and dropping epochs with outlying power. Depression is reported to alter slow alpha and theta envelope coupling, which spectral coherence (phase and amplitude consistency per segment) doesn't capture. The block is small (76 features, the same size as Hjorth), so it shouldn't dilute the existing features, and it is independent of amplitude scale.

This round adds one small, scale-invariant block that measures how stable each subject's EEG state is over the recording, which every current feature averages away. For theta and alpha, it takes the robust spread (IQR/1.349) of the log relative band power across 2-s spectrogram segments, per channel and condition. The motivation is the vigilance-regulation model of depression (Hegerl, VIGALL), which reports "hyperstable" vigilance in MDD: alpha drifts and theta intrusions from drowsiness are less frequent than in controls. The block adds 76 features, the same size as Hjorth and AEC, which both helped, and the quartile-based spread keeps it robust to artifacts.

Theta/alpha amplitude-envelope correlation (AEC) node strength helped in round 16. This round extends it to the beta band (13–30 Hz), adding 38 scale-invariant features. Beta envelope coupling reflects fronto-parietal top-down and ruminative network activity that is reported altered in MDD, and neither beta coherence nor beta power captures it.

Add a second aperiodic exponent per channel and condition, fitted over 20–45 Hz on the same median Welch PSD. In Gao et al. (2017), the high-frequency spectral slope tracks the excitation/inhibition balance, which is reported altered in MDD. The current 2–40 Hz fit is dominated by the low-frequency part of the spectrum, so it mostly misses this. The new block is small (38 features), needs no epoch-level computation, and is amplitude-scale invariant.

I'm adding detrended fluctuation analysis (DFA) exponents of the theta and alpha amplitude envelopes for each channel and condition. Linkenkaer-Hansen et al. (2005) reported weakened long-range temporal correlations of theta and alpha oscillations in MDD. This 76-feature block measures how oscillation amplitude persists over 1–20 s, which none of the current features capture, and it does not depend on amplitude scale. The theta and alpha Hilbert envelopes are now computed once and shared by the AEC and DFA blocks, so the AEC features are unchanged.
